system_overview: This specification models the behavior of correct processes in an eventually perfect failure detector, based on the framework of Chandra and Toueg (1996) for unreliable failure detectors in reliable distributed systems. Each process periodically sends alive messages to all other processes, periodically makes predictions about which processes have crashed, and receives messages from others. Predictions are based on whether a process has heard from another process within an adaptive timeout interval.
actors_and_components: The system consists of a set of processes, each of which acts as both a sender and a receiver. Each process has a local clock, maintains a suspicion list of processes it believes have crashed, tracks adaptive timeout intervals for each other process, and records how long it has been since it last heard from each other process. Processes periodically send alive messages and periodically evaluate their suspicion lists.
state_variables: For each process, the system tracks: (1) A suspicion set -- which other processes it currently suspects of having crashed. (2) A timeout interval for each other process -- the duration it waits before suspecting that process. (3) A counter for each other process tracking how many ticks since last hearing from that process. (4) A local clock value (integer). (5) A set of outgoing messages that the process wants to send in the current transition. The sending and predicting operations are separated by local clock timing: a process sends alive messages at every multiple of a send interval, and makes predictions at every multiple of a predict interval, with these two intervals constrained to never coincide.
initial_state: No process suspects any other process of having crashed. All timeout intervals are set to a default value. All last-heard counters are zero (all processes are considered recently heard from). All local clocks start at zero. No outgoing messages exist.
actions: Three main process actions, determined by the local clock: (1) Send alive: When the local clock is at a multiple of the send interval (but not the predict interval), the process creates alive messages addressed to every other process, places them in its outgoing message set, increments its local clock, and increments last-heard counters for processes it has not yet timed out on. (2) Predict: When the local clock is at a multiple of the predict interval (but not the send interval), the process adds to its suspicion set any process from which it has not heard for longer than the corresponding timeout interval. It increments last-heard counters and its local clock. (3) Receive: At all other clock values, the process receives incoming messages. For each process from which it receives an alive message, it resets the corresponding last-heard counter to zero and removes that process from its suspicion set. If a suspected process sends a message that is received, the timeout interval for that process is increased by one (adaptive timeout). The local clock is reset to zero when it exceeds all relevant thresholds (send interval, predict interval, and all timeout intervals), creating a finite clock domain.
safety_properties: Type invariant: Last-heard counters are integers. Timeout intervals are integers. Suspicion sets are subsets of the process set. Outgoing messages are subsets of the message type.
additional_assumptions: The send interval and predict interval must both be positive and must not be multiples of each other, ensuring that send and predict operations never happen simultaneously. This module is designed to be instantiated by a controller that manages the communication channel and environmental clock. The adaptive timeout mechanism ensures that correct processes are eventually no longer suspected.
